newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Hong Kong banks borrow more.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - Hong Kong banks borrow more.

text.p: Asian debt markets were busy with Hong Kong dollar issues on Thursday.
Bank of East Asia launched a HK$2.6 billion floating rate certificate of deposit issue. The three-year paper pays a margin of 30 basis points and, with fees, an all-in of 37 basis points.
Bank of East Asia is rated A3 by Moody's Investors Service.
Application will be made to the Hong Kong Monetary Authority to accept the certificates as eligible for its Liquidity Adjustment Facility, or discount window.
Bank of East Asia paid 44 basis points all-in for three years for its last FRCD launched in October 1996.

"We will see whether this issue is accepted as the new benchmark pricing," remarked one syndicate manager, who added that his bank would be joining the deal because the issue offers a better return than other LAF issues launched recently.
Societe Generale Asia and UBS are the arrangers.
First Pacific Bank launched a HK$500 million equivalent FRCD issue that is available in Hong Kong and U.S. dollars tranches.
Both tranches mature in five years but can be put or called on the third and fourth anniversaries.
The Hong Kong dollar tranche pays a margin of 60 basis points over HIBOR and the U.S. dollar tranche offers a margin of 40 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate.
Fees are 78 basis points to top-tier participants, giving an all-in of 86 basis points for Hong Kong dollars and an all-in of 66 basis points for U.S. dollars.
WestLB, CS First Boston, Bayerische Landesbank and Standard Chartered Bank are the arrangers.
DKB Asia privately placed a couple of Hong Kong dollar FRCDs for local banks. Dah Sing Bank sold HK$200 million one-year FRCDs that pay a coupon of 25 basis points.
Hong Kong's GE Capital Finance, a unit of General Electric Capital Corp, issued HK$50 million in FRCDs. The two-year paper pays a coupon of 30 basis points.
Today's Hong Kong dollar deals joins a long list of issues launched recently.
Bankers said there are many reasons for the flush of new issues. Some banks, for example, are simply refinancing and many are taking advantage of the market's good tone.

Some syndicate managers have speculated that local borrowers may want to get their funding out of the way before the July 1 handover of Hong Kong to China just in case there is some market volatility around the time of the transfer.
But others pointed out that Hong Kong borrowers have been able to borrow much more cheaply this year, at least in part because of confidence about the handover.

Moreover, added a syndicate manager at a local bank, bankers for some time have been eager to lend three- to five-year money to Hong Kong institutions, a time period that exposes them to Hong Kong risk long after the handover.
